summary.text: A nine-year-old male, previously asymptomatic, presented to the emergency department with a headache that had persisted for one month and no other symptoms. Examination showed severe short stature, Tanner stage I, no goitre and no neurological findings, and laboratory tests including complete blood count and blood glucose were normal. Brain MRI and a dedicated sella MRI showed pituitary enlargement interpreted as a pituitary adenoma.

Pediatric endocrinology measured TSH, free T4 and cortisol, finding a markedly elevated TSH of 936 mIU/L, a suppressed free T4 below 0.4 ng/dL and a normal morning cortisol. The case was discussed with neurosurgery, and given the markedly elevated TSH, thyroid hormone replacement therapy was initiated, with re-evaluation planned once thyroid function normalised.

Once TSH and free T4 were within normal limits, a follow-up sella MRI three months later showed a completely normal pituitary gland. Case review identified pituitary hyperplasia secondary to thyroid dysfunction mimicking an adenoma. No adverse events were reported during levothyroxine therapy, and the patient remained on replacement with periodic monitoring and no dose adjustment.

Levothyroxine dose and route are not stated.
Discussion recommendations (for example a three-month follow-up MRI) are general guidance and not patient facts.
